title: Reading notes - LLM inference (Sophie Kim)
content:
Quick personal reading notes and scratchpad on LLM inference optimizations - intended to capture takeaways, ideas to try on Redwood sandbox, and TODOs. Mostly raw/fragments.

Context / goals:
- Understand practical wins for 2-10x inference cost/latency reductions that are realistic to deploy (quant, batching, caching, kernel-level optimizations).
- Prioritize experiments for Dedicated/private customers: where we can guarantee latency + reduce cost.

Papers / posts I skimmed (high level):
- FlashAttention / flash-attention implementations (fast attention GPU kernels) - pragmatic: large reduction in memory + faster attention by tiling; good for long sequences. See GitHub + follow-up optimizations (FlashAttention2/FlashWAttention). Notes: integration complexity depends on tokenizer/seq lengths and current runtime kernel system.
- 8-bit and mixed-precision quantization posts (GPTQ, LLM.int8/xformers approaches) - big perf/cost wins without large quality loss for many tasks; watch out for outliers (sensitive prompts). Practical thought: maintain two flavors of models (quantized for cheap/bulk, fp16 for high-quality/canary).
- KV-cache / prefix-cache caching strategies (various engineering blog posts) - automatic prefix KV caching yields substantial token-cost savings for interactive chat where users repeat context. Need good eviction and consistency with rolling updates.
- Batching strategies - continuous batching vs synchronous batching: tradeoff between throughput and tail latency. Some papers highlight adaptive batching that respects SLOs. For Redwood Dedicated, we can expose batching knobs per route.

My quick summaries / takeaways:
- Kernel-level wins (FlashAttention et al.) are huge but require careful integration testing. For on-prem/private installs we can provide an optimized build. For Hosted API, we can test optimized builds in a canary pool.
- Quantization is the most direct cost lever. However:
  - Need per-model eval prompts to detect quality regressions (link to Redwood Optimize idea).
  - Consider hybrid: maintain a fast-quant model plus a fallback to fp16 for low-confidence outputs.
- KV-caching is low-hanging fruit for many chat products: prefix caching + response caching for repeated prompts could cut token-generation cost dramatically. But caching semantics + privacy/segmenting per-customer matter.
- Batching: for low-latency services we should offer an SLO-aware batching policy: e.g., target 95th latency and let batcher adapt. Also allow developers to opt-out for strict latency.

Notes about deployment complexity / safety:
- Rolling upgrades with quantized models: need model ver semantics + ability to A/B. Ensure we can fallback quickly.
- For private deployments, provide an "optimized inference bundle" (prebuilt runtime with FlashAttention, tuned kernel selection) + docs. Might be a paid add-on.

Ideas to try (short experiment list):
1) Small sandbox: deploy quantized Llama-2-7B variant to a Dedicated-like pool and run Redwood internal eval prompts (safety/quality). Compare latency + token-cost. (Linked artifact: JIRA INF-1423)
2) KV-cache follow-up: implement TTL and prefix-based invalidation; test on sample chat logs (customer anonymized). Measure hit rate and token reduction.
3) Adaptive batching sim: build a synthetic load generator (90/95/99 latency targets) and evaluate throughput vs 95th tail for different batch strategies.
4) Canary optimized kernel: compile runtime with FlashAttention and run A/B vs baseline on 7B/13B for throughput/latency. Watch memory regressions.

Practical notes / snippets:
- "Notes to self": when quantizing, keep a dev-only rollback path and keep per-prompt QA checks. Track LM perplexity + key eval prompts.
- Logging: need prompt-level tooling to mark which model variant served, quant flags, and batch size - makes rollback diagnostics possible.
- Cost accounting: tag tokens by model flavor (quant vs fp16) in analytics so Optimize can recommend when to switch.

Open questions / unresolved:
- How much of FlashAttention gains are already captured by our current kernel selector? (ACTION: ask infra team for current kernel map.)
- Are there public benchmarks for quantized 13B QW/LLM.int8 that we can baseline against?
- For caching, what's the best privacy-preserving approach for multi-tenant Dedicated? (per-tenant caches vs per-instance)

Useful links I want to keep around:
- FlashAttention repo: https://github.com/flash-attention/flash-attention
- GPTQ / quantization community repos (bookmark)
- Blog posts: NVidia mixed-precision guides, Hugging Face quantization logs

TODOs / next steps (short):
- Add experimental plan to Confluence (eng-applied-ml/kv-cache-playbook) - assign owners.
- Create JIRA tickets for sandbox quantization + canary kernel build. (INF-1423 + INF-1424)
- Quick sync with infra/runtime owner (Ben or Aisha) to check kernel integration constraints.

Random personal notes: messy thoughts below - ignore for others unless asked:
- Could expose an "economy mode" flag in API that routes to quantized + aggressive batching + caching with obvious warnings in dashboard.
- Evaluate if we can provide a "quality knob" (e.g., target logprob threshold to trigger fallback to fp16).

End of notes. Intend to clean and move relevant parts to Confluence and JIRA once experiments are scheduled.
